note: The weekly loop's first challengers, from the research (18 Nov 2026): what the research was unsure of, ranked, alternating first-second and look tests.

candidates.test: Shorts whose second and third lines go straight into the machine working (the 'how' answered with a moving part by 6 s: 'How? Its machines were 150 metres long and built the tunnel as they dug'), with no year, inventor backstory or historical figure before 10 s, against the champion, where the line after the question may open on a date or a record ('In 1945, radar engineer Percy Spencer...', 'Historically, it made up to 2,074 megawatts')
candidates.why: Our own retention: both Shorts with a curve lost their biggest share at 7.5 s, exactly on the line that turned to backstory: the microwave fell from 81% to 52% on 'In 1945, radar engineer Percy Spencer felt the chocolate...', Hoover Dam from 100% to 81% on 'Historically, it made up to 2,074 megawatts'. The Crossrail Short, whose second line was the machine itself, has 1,362 views in its first day, 5x our next best (284). References agree: 'How a Dam Generates Electricity' (AI Tech 3.7, 8.7M views on 11K subscribers, 41 s) is inside the intake at 0 s with no history; Inside Decoded's 'This computer had no chips' gives the twist at 2.4 s and the date only at 5-12 s. Two curves only, so medium confidence; placed first among first-second tests because it comes from our own drop points.

candidates.test: the payoff's figure as a picture in the first 3 s (a line diving to a number) against the champion's picture-first open
candidates.why: ColdFusion opens on the figure; only 11% of the niche's Shorts show a figure by 3 s

candidates.test: a 3D character skit Short against the champion zoom/invention Short
candidates.why: AI skits median 1.14M, but all 81 from one channel (Professor Of AI); needs the 3D character

candidates.test: 30-40 s Shorts against the 45-60 s champion
candidates.why: the scan's 20-35 s band hits 21% vs 11-12% at 35-70 s; the references run 58-97 s

candidates.test: a look morph (textured -> wireframe -> clay -> textured) as the opening picture
candidates.why: the owner's favourite reference opens on it

candidates.test: a contradiction slammed in big at 0.5 s ('NO CHIPS') instead of the question line
candidates.why: Inside Decoded's water-computer Short opens this way; 2 of 19 references

candidates.test: a light, clean studio stage instead of the dark one
candidates.why: Branch Education's Shorts mix light gradient stages; the dark stage is the champion from the long references

candidates.test: titles that name the thing in the third person, with no 'you' or 'your' ('Why Keyboards Aren't in ABC Order'), against titles that address the viewer ('Why Your Keyboard Isn't in ABC Order')
candidates.why: Niche scan of 3,594 tech Shorts (niche-data 2026-11-18): titles with you/your have a median 0.81x their channel's median views and 20% hits (n=426) against 1.02x and 31% without; lower inside 19 of 29 channels that use both (Inside Decoded 0.46x vs 1.71x over 31 titles). Three of our open topics use 'Your'. Views are the evidence; the loop judges it on stayed to watch.

candidates.test: invention Shorts titled as a numbered series ('The Inventions Inside Every Phone, Part 3: The Transistor') against the champion's single claim title
candidates.why: Numbered-series titles: 1.46x channel median, 44% hits (n=25) against 1.0x and 30%; higher inside 4 of 5 channels that use them. Logibu's 'Most Important Invention In History, Part N' reached 5.35M and 3.96M on 36K subscribers. Mostly one channel, so low confidence.

candidates.test: Shorts told as the small-to-giant shape (an everyday thing the viewer holds, stepped up through real machines to the giant one) against the champion's one-thing-all-the-way-down story
candidates.why: You Built A... (12K subscribers) runs every Short this way: 'How a Stack of Bricks Becomes a Skyscraper' 2.53M views (211x its subscribers), its next 11 at 62K-508K (5-42x) in the 18 Nov niche scan. One channel only and 100-130 s long, so low confidence; placed last among first-second tests.
